## References

1. [Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks (Time Horizon)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14499)

# Notes

## The problem this paper solves

We have no good unit for "how capable is this AI agent?" Benchmarks give you a percentage — "Claude scores 70% on SWE-bench" — but a percentage is meaningless on its own. 70% of *what*? It saturates the moment a model passes it, it's adversarially curated toward whatever current models can't do, and it doesn't let you compare a 2023 model to a 2025 model on the same ruler. Worst of all, a benchmark score doesn't translate into any human-intuitive claim about *what work the agent could actually replace*.

METR's move is to change the unit. Instead of measuring **accuracy on a fixed task set**, they measure **task length, in units of how long a skilled human takes**. The core object is the **50%-task-completion time horizon**: the human-time-length of tasks that an AI can complete with 50% reliability. If a model has a "50-minute time horizon," it means: take the set of tasks that a competent human does in ~50 minutes, and the model succeeds at about half of them. This is a single number, in minutes, that you can track across years and across models — and it has an immediate, legible meaning ("this agent can do roughly hour-long chunks of software work").

The payoff finding: this number has been **doubling roughly every 7 months since 2019**. That is the headline, and the whole paper is the scaffolding required to make that one number trustworthy.

## The core idea, built up slowly

Step 1 — **anchor difficulty to human time, not to a benchmark's internal score.** For every task in their suite, they recruit skilled humans (domain experts who do *not* know the specific task/codebase ahead of time), have them actually attempt it, and record how long the successful completions take. That wall-clock time becomes the task's "length." So a task isn't "hard" because a benchmark author labeled it hard; it's "30 minutes long" because that's how long humans took. They collected **800+ human baselines** to set these lengths.

Step 2 — **run AI agents on the same tasks and record binary success/failure.** Each model attempts each task in an agent scaffold (it can run code, read output, retry, use tools). You get a grid: for each (model, task) pair, a 0 or 1.

Step 3 — **fit a curve from task-length to success-probability, per model.** Now plot, for one model, success (0/1) against the human-time length of the task (on a log axis). Long tasks → mostly failures; short tasks → mostly successes. Fit a **logistic curve** through this cloud. The model's **50% time horizon** is simply the task-length where that fitted curve crosses 50% success. Read it off the x-axis.

Step 4 — **plot each model's horizon against its release date, on a log axis.** The points fall on a remarkably straight line → exponential growth → constant doubling time (~7 months).

That's the entire logic. Everything else is making each step defensible.

## The logistic model, symbol by symbol

The fit is psychometrics-flavored — it borrows from **Item Response Theory (IRT)**, where each "item" (task) has a difficulty and each "subject" (here, a model) has an ability. The relationship modeled is roughly:

`P(success | task) = sigmoid( β · (h − t) )`

reading the symbols:
- `t` = the **task's difficulty**, operationalized as `log(human completion time)`. Using log-time is essential: capability gains feel multiplicative (going from 1-min to 10-min tasks is "one step," 10-min to 100-min is "the next step"), so the natural x-axis is logarithmic.
- `h` = the model's **50% time horizon**, on the same log scale — this is the *fitted parameter you care about*. It's the value of `t` where the linear predictor `β·(h − t)` equals zero, i.e. where `P(success) = sigmoid(0) = 0.5`. So `h` is literally defined as the crossover point.
- `β` = the **slope** of the logistic — how sharply success collapses as tasks get longer. A steep `β` means a crisp cliff (the model does everything below its horizon and nothing above); a shallow `β` means a gradual rolloff.
- `sigmoid(x) = 1 / (1 + e^(−x))`.

To get the **80% time horizon**, you solve for the `t` where `P = 0.8` instead of `0.5`. Because the logistic is monotone decreasing in task length, the 80% horizon is always shorter than the 50% horizon — empirically **about 5× shorter**. That gap matters: a model with a 50-min *50%* horizon only does ~10-min tasks *reliably* (80%). Reliability costs you roughly an order of magnitude of task length.

## The exponential trend fit

With one horizon `h` per model, the second regression is a simple line in log-space:

`log(time_horizon) = a + b · (release_date)`

- `b` is the growth rate. The **doubling time** is `log(2) / b` (in whatever date units `b` uses) — and that comes out to **≈ 7 months**.
- `a` is the intercept (the implied horizon at the start of the window).

The fit is strikingly clean — the reported R² across 2019–2025 is very high (~0.98 in the headline regression), which is part of why the result drew so much attention: the points really do lie on a line across six years and ~13 frontier models. METR puts a **95% CI on the doubling time via hierarchical bootstrap** (resampling both tasks and baselines) rather than treating the fit as noise-free.

## The numbers — models, the reliability boundary, validation

**Per-model 50% horizons (chronological, approximate):**
- **GPT-2 (2019): ~2 seconds.** It can barely do anything an agent would call a "task."
- **GPT-3 / early GPT-3.5:** seconds to tens of seconds.
- **GPT-4 (0314, March 2023): ~5–8 minutes.** Early GPT-4 variants cluster around the 4–8 minute mark.
- **GPT-4o, Claude 3 Opus, Claude 3.5 Sonnet:** tens of minutes, climbing.
- **o1 / reasoning-trained models (late 2024):** a clear jump — part of the *possible 2024 acceleration* the paper flags.
- **Claude 3.7 Sonnet (early 2025): ~50 minutes** — the v1 frontier figure.
- (Later versions / follow-ups push this further: **o3 ≈ 1.5–2 hours**, and subsequent frontier models even higher — but the v1 paper's frontier anchor is the ~50-minute Claude 3.7 Sonnet number.)

**The reliability boundary** is a vivid way to read the same data: current frontier models are at **near-100% success on tasks humans do in under ~4 minutes**, but drop to **under ~10% success on tasks that take humans more than ~4 hours**. The "interesting" regime — where models go from usually-succeeding to usually-failing — is exactly the band their horizon sits in.

**External validation on SWE-bench Verified.** They replicate the method on real GitHub PR tasks (with human *time estimates* rather than fresh baselines) and find the *same exponential shape* — in fact a **faster doubling time of under ~3 months**. And the **2023–2025 growth rate matches the 2019–2025 rate to within ~11%**, arguing the trend isn't an artifact of the early, easy years.

**Robustness.** They apply **10,000 random perturbations** to the data (dropping tasks, reweighting, jittering baselines) and report the resulting distribution over "date AI reaches a 1-month horizon," plus subset analyses (by length, by task suite, by messiness). The doubling time is not very sensitive to any single methodological choice they tried.

## What's actually driving the gains

The paper's qualitative read: the improvement is **not** mainly raw reasoning IQ. It's **reliability and error-recovery** — the ability to notice a mistake, adapt, and not derail an hour-long chain of actions — combined with better tool use and longer coherent logical chains. Short tasks were already solved; the frontier is moving because models can now *sustain* correct behavior over more sequential steps without compounding failure. (This connects to the multiplicative-failure intuition below: a longer task is a longer product of per-step success probabilities, so even small per-step reliability gains buy disproportionate length.)

## The 170-task suite

Three sources, deliberately spanning seconds to tens of hours:
- **HCAST** — broad software/cyber/reasoning agentic tasks (the bulk of the medium-length range).
- **RE-Bench** — hard ML-research-engineering tasks (the long tail, hours-long).
- **SWAA (Software Atomic Actions)** — **66 novel very short tasks** (seconds to ~minutes). These exist specifically so that ancient models like GPT-2/GPT-3 register a *non-zero, measurable* horizon — without them, pre-2023 models would just score ~0 everywhere and you couldn't anchor the left end of the trend line.

## The "messiness" critique — the real weak point

This is the most important limitation, and the authors themselves flag it. Their tasks are **clean**: well-specified, with clear success criteria, reversible actions, and tight feedback loops. Real economically valuable work is **messy**. In an appendix they score every HCAST/RE-Bench task (those ≥1 minute) on **16 "messiness" factors** — properties that make real tasks harder for agents, e.g.:
- you can make **irreversible mistakes**,
- you **consume limited resources** on each attempt,
- you **can't cleanly attribute outcomes** to your own actions vs. external causes,
- you **can't easily measure** whether you've succeeded,
- the task is under-specified / the spec drifts.

The damning numbers: the **mean messiness of their tasks is 3.2/16, and none exceeds 8/16.** For calibration, "write a good research paper" would score ~9–15/16. So the suite lives in the *clean* corner of task-space. And critically, **when they split tasks into messiest-vs-cleanest halves, performance on the messy half collapses — no model tops ~30% success on the messiest 50% of tasks.** This is the crux of the external-validity worry: the 7-month doubling is measured on tidy tasks, and the trend may bend (or the horizons may be inflated) for the messy real-world work the extrapolation is supposed to be about. METR's own later follow-up reinforced this — a large fraction of agent-generated SWE-bench PRs would be **rejected by real maintainers**, so "task passed the automated check" overstates real usefulness.

## Genuine limitations (beyond messiness)

- **Asymmetric protocol.** Humans baseline under an 8-hour cap; AIs effectively had no time limit. Different stopping rules muddy the "equivalent" comparison.
- **Sparse long-task data.** In the task-length band that determines a frontier model's horizon, there are only ~14 relevant samples — so getting 1–2 extra long tasks right *materially* moves the headline number. The horizon estimate is fragile exactly where it matters most.
- **Is logistic even the right curve?** If a task of length L is "succeed on each of ~L independent steps," success is a **product** of per-step probabilities → an **exponential** rolloff in length, not a logistic one (a point raised by Toby Ord). Once you *assume* a logistic, a new model solving one more long task almost mechanically extends the log-linear trend — so the clean line is partly baked in by the functional-form choice.
- **Extrapolation confounds.** Projecting "1-month tasks in ~5 years" assumes the curve doesn't bend. But the slope itself could change from agency-specific training, more inference-time compute, or AI starting to automate AI R&D — any of which could speed it up or, conversely, the messiness wall could slow it down.
- **Domain experts ≠ codebase experts.** Baseliners knew the domain but not the specific codebase, which may inflate human times (and therefore the apparent task "length" the AI is credited with).

## Positioning vs. prior work and the safety frame

Prior agentic evals (SWE-bench, GAIA, etc.) report **pass-rates on fixed sets** that saturate and don't yield a cross-time scalar. METR's contribution is the **reparameterization into human-time horizons + a fitted growth law**, turning scattered benchmark points into a single forecastable trend with a doubling time. It's a *measurement-and-forecasting* paper, not a method/training paper.

For the dangerous-capabilities / control agenda, time horizon is a natural **capability axis to govern against**: the length of autonomous task an agent can sustain is precisely what determines whether it could carry out a long, multi-step harmful or self-exfiltrating plan, and whether a human-in-the-loop can realistically oversee it. The reliability-over-long-horizons story is the same property that makes long-horizon autonomy *dangerous*, which is why this metric matters to the case that powerful agentic AIs need to be deliberately controlled — see [[Shlegeris Greenblatt - The Case for Ensuring Powerful AIs are Controlled]]. The control-evaluation literature ([[AI Control - Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion]], [[Ctrl-Z - Controlling AI Agents via Resampling]]) studies whether oversight protocols hold up against a capable, possibly-scheming agent across an extended task; the time-horizon curve quantifies *how extended* that task can be and how fast that envelope is expanding — i.e., it tells the control agenda how much runway it has before agents can sustain the kind of long, multi-step autonomy that those protocols are built to contain.

## One-line takeaway

By redefining capability as "the human-time-length of tasks an agent can do at 50% reliability," METR converts noisy benchmark scores into a single, legible number that has doubled every ~7 months for six years — a clean trend whose biggest asterisk is that it's measured on tidy tasks (mean messiness 3.2/16) while the world's valuable work is messy.
